messages.subject: t-test
parts:
The following example was taken from "Introduction to WinBUGS for Ecologists" by Kery (Academic Press 2010) and translated into Stan.
-------------------------------------------------------------ch_7_2.R----------------------------------------
library(rstan)

set.seed(12345)

n1 <- 60                # Number of females
n2 <- 40                # Number of males
mu1 <- 105                # Population mean of females
mu2 <- 77.5                # Population mean of males
sigma <- 2.75                # Average population SD of both

n <- n1+n2                # Total sample size
y1 <- rnorm(n1, mu1, sigma)        # Data for females
y2 <- rnorm(n2, mu2, sigma)        # Date for males
y <- c(y1, y2)                # Aggregate both data sets
x <- rep(c(0,1), c(n1, n2))        # Indicator for male

ch7_2_data <- list(n1=n1, n2=n2, x=x, y1=y1, y2=y2)

fit <- stan(file="ch7_2.stan", data=ch7_2_data, warmup=1000, iter=21000)

print(fit, digits=3)
-------------------------------------------------------------ch_7_2.R----------------------------------------

The Stan code is:
-------------------------------------------------------------ch_7_2.stan----------------------------------------
data {
     int<lower=0> n1;
     int<lower=0> n2;
     real y1[n1];
     real y2[n2];
}
parameters {
           real alpha1;
           real alpha2;
           real<lower=0> sigma1;
           real<lower=0> sigma2;
}
model {
      for (n in 1:n1)
          y1[n] ~ normal(alpha1, sigma1);
      for (n in 1:n2)
          y2[n] ~ normal(alpha2, sigma2);
}
generated quantities {
          real dif;
          dif <- sigma1 - sigma2;
}
-------------------------------------------------------------ch_7_2.stan----------------------------------------

Here are the outputs:

> print(fit, digits=3)
Inference for Stan model: ch7_2.
4 chains: each with iter=21000; warmup=1000; thin=1; 21000 iterations saved.

           mean se_mean    sd     2.5%      25%      50%      75%    97.5%
alpha1  105.532   0.006 0.408  104.719  105.259  105.536  105.810  106.319
alpha2   78.381   0.003 0.508   77.382   78.046   78.383   78.715   79.378
sigma1    3.136   0.018 0.299    2.626    2.933    3.108    3.302    3.807
sigma2    3.192   0.019 0.376    2.557    2.922    3.160    3.420    4.026
dif      -0.056   0.025 0.476   -1.000   -0.364   -0.049    0.262    0.869
lp__   -161.172   0.051 1.467 -164.917 -161.889 -160.831 -160.095 -159.370
       n_eff  Rhat
alpha1  4972 1.000
alpha2 21972 1.000
sigma1   286 1.004
sigma2   374 1.008
dif      361 1.007
lp__     835 1.003

Samples were drawn using NUTS2 at Tue Oct 16 13:04:54 2012.
For each parameter, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size,
and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at
convergence, Rhat=1).

My question is: why the estimated sigma values (3.136 and 3.192) are much larger than their assigned value (2.75)? Are there something wrong with my code?

Many thanks.

Best,
Shige

parts:
On Tuesday, October 16, 2012 1:24:43 PM UTC-4, Shige wrote:
My question is: why the estimated sigma values (3.136 and 3.192) are much larger than their assigned value (2.75)? Are there something wrong with my code?

I think your code is not wrong (although we would much prefer attachments than embedding everything in a post).

You can speed it up considerably by vectorizing the normals, as in

model {
    y1 ~ normal(alpha1, sigma1);          
    y2 ~ normal(alpha2, sigma2);
}

Stan is not getting a great effective sample size on these standard deviation estimates, but they are close to what you would get from least squares, e.g. in R

> summary(lm(y1 ~ 1)); summary(lm(y2 ~ 1))

Call:
lm(formula = y1 ~ 1)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max
-7.0827 -1.9017  0.4564  1.7145  5.5045

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 105.5368     0.3983     265   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Residual standard error: 3.085 on 59 degrees of freedom


Call:
lm(formula = y2 ~ 1)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max
-5.9196 -2.5952  0.5678  1.8247  5.9315

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  78.3806     0.4843   161.8   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Residual standard error: 3.063 on 39 degrees of freedom

So, I think the basic answer is that the simulation does not have much data and the 12345 seed gave you two somewhat extreme draws for the data. That, and with small sample sizes, the absence of informative priors on the parameters can make a difference.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: t-test (effects of initialization)
parts:
On 10/16/12 3:32 PM, Shige Song wrote:
> Thanks for the help, Ben. Dropping the seed did lead to closer estimates of the sigma.

There's always a seed. If you don't specify one, Stan
generates it randomly given the time.

> I did not expect setting random
> number seed can have such an effect.

It comes down to the initialization. If you do
your own initial points, it won't matter nearly
as much for sampling. But random inits, especially
with weak constraints, can lead to very bad initial
points that take a lot of time to adapt out of.

If you run long enough, adaptation should find a
better place and adapt to that before sampling.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: t-test (effects of initialization)
parts:

On 10/16/12 3:32 PM, Shige Song wrote:
> Thanks for the help, Ben. Dropping the seed did lead to closer estimates of the sigma.

There's always a seed.  If you don't specify one, Stan
generates it randomly given the time.

What Bob said is true for command-line Stan. The stan() function in the RStan package passes a seed from R to Stan, but by default, that is just a function of the state of R's pseduo-random number generator, which was explicitly set in this case.

Ben

On Tuesday, October 16, 2012 4:37:21 PM UTC-4, Shige wrote:
Can you be more specific about how to vectorize the model for this particular case? Thanks.
The original model {} block was

model {
      for (n in 1:n1)
          y1[n] ~ normal(alpha1, sigma1);
      for (n in 1:n2)
          y2[n] ~ normal(alpha2, sigma2);
}
This style is necessary for BUGS but involves n1 + n2 function calls. In Stan you can write it as

model {
    y1 ~ normal(alpha1, sigma1);          
    y2 ~ normal(alpha2, sigma2);
}

which is only two function calls and has several other optimizations. We also have a FAQ about optimizing speed that includes a section on vectorization.

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/4gv3fNCqSNk/J6ZItL2ZJ-IJ

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: t-test
parts:
On 10/16/12 4:45 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Tuesday, October 16, 2012 4:37:21 PM UTC-4, Shige wrote:
>
> Can you be more specific about how to vectorize the model for this particular case? Thanks.
>
>
> The original model {} block was
>
> |
> model {
> for (n in 1:n1)
> y1[n] ~ normal(alpha1, sigma1);
> for (n in 1:n2)
> y2[n] ~ normal(alpha2, sigma2);
> }
> |
>
> This style is necessary for BUGS but involves n1 + n2 function calls.

The real issue is what those function calls (to normal_log(y1[n],alpha1,sigma1))
do. Non-virtual function calls like this are pretty fast.

The problem is that every time you involve an expression
in the log probability calculation, you wind up allocating
memory for the expression in the expression tree stack,
calling its constructor (which can involve some copies by
reference) and then evaluating the virtual function call
for the chain rule during the gradient calculation.

What happens in the vectorized version is that one compound
expression gets put on the expression tree stack and
only one constructor is called and one virtual function for
the chain rule applied to the node during auto-dif. There's
also less pointer chasing within the chain rule and more
locality because the vector data's stored contiguously as
double types.

On top of that, if all the arguments are not vectors,
some redundant calculations can be eliminated by some
algebra up front.

In Stan you can write it as
>
> |
> model {
> y1 ~ normal(alpha1, sigma1);
> y2 ~ normal(alpha2, sigma2);
> }
> |
>
> which is only two function calls and has several other optimizations.

See above :-)

- Bob

It did not take long for the program to run but the results (out.txt) are quite surprising: the "n_eff" is 2 for five of the six coefficients. On Saturday, October 20, 2012 7:40:18 AM UTC-4, Shige wrote:
I did some more experiments. This time, I increased the sample size from 60 and 40 to 60,000 and 40,000 to see how well Stan handles data of this size. It did not take long for the program to run but the results (out.txt) are quite surprising: the "n_eff" is 2 for five of the six coefficients. One would expect with 20,000 iterations and 10,000 warmup, the results should be rather  stable.

By the way, I am running the most recent git version of rstan.

Here at Stan World Headquarters, we have actually been working with your example for a few days but with 600 and 400 observations. A few bugs in rstan have been fixed and we will probably release v1.0.3 next week. But the basic problem in your case is that by default, Stan starts with uniform draws of the parameters from the [-2,2] interval. In your case, the true means are 105 and 77.5, which is very far away. If you look at

> lp <- get_logposterior(fit, inc_warmup = TRUE)
> sapply(lp, head)
              [,1]           [,2]         [,3]          [,4]
[1,] -38854764.995 -201405126.509 -6473613.053 -41854200.654
[2,]     -5119.183      -5054.171    -5037.778     -6651.749
[3,]     -5039.239      -5053.858    -5036.749     -5030.744
[4,]     -5040.267      -5054.297    -5007.958     -5030.275
[5,]     -5038.682      -5054.230    -4998.652     -5030.858
[6,]     -5039.415      -5053.292    -3915.622     -5030.384


you can see that the first iteration is just awful for all four chains. The next few iterations are much, much better but still really, really bad compared to the truth which is around -1500.  And sometimes one or more of the chains never makes it to the mode. We hope to do better, but maybe not in the next (few) release(s).

In the meantime, you can either standardize the input or provide reasonable initial values. Both of those should work fine regardless of the number of observations.

Ben
